1:
Henry reads the register as a recruiting poster. Ezra, having his commission from the king, beats up for volunteers and sets up an ensign to assemble the outcasts of Israel: whoever among the sons of Zion, dwelling with the daughters of Babylon, is disposed to go to Jerusalem, now that the house there is finished and its service set going, now is their time. What strikes Henry is how few came. He cannot understand how any of them could read the prophet's summons to shake off the dust and loose the bands of the neck and still stay behind, and he names the reason without softening it: they loved their ease better than their religion, thought themselves well off where they were, and either did not believe Jerusalem would better their condition or dared not face the journey. The heads of families are set down here, Henry says, for their honour, and the males they brought amount to fourteen hundred and ninety-six.

Henry also notices who travelled light. Two priests are named and one of the house of David, and it seems they came without their families — intending, perhaps, to see how they liked Jerusalem and then either send for them or go back. Several of the clans named here had already sent a company home in the first return; some went then, more now, as God inclined their hearts. Henry will not make the latecomers second-class: some were called into the vineyard at the third hour and others not till the eleventh, yet even those were not rejected.

Ellicott states the principle on which the whole list is built — the name of the head of a house is generally followed by that of the wider family he belonged to — and directs the reader to compare it with the earlier register of those who returned under Zerubbabel. Clarke, who gives the chapter's whole argument in a paragraph before touching a word of it, adds the small distinctions that keep the names apart: there are three men called Shechaniah in this book, and they are told apart by their fathers' houses.

The two priestly names draw a caution. Gill is emphatic that the Daniel here is not the prophet, who was of royal blood and of the tribe of Judah; this Daniel was a priest, descended from Ithamar, as Gershom was of Eleazar in the line of Phinehas. Clarke says the same of Gershom in a line. Delitzsch turns the point into a rule of reading: Gershom and Daniel are heads of priestly houses, and sons of Phinehas and sons of Ithamar are designations of races, not parentage. He guards against a false inference too — the verse does not mean that only two priests went up with Ezra, since twelve chief priests were chosen later to take charge of the treasure. Whether this Daniel is the one named among the priests in the later covenant list, Delitzsch says plainly, does not appear.

The register is also damaged, and both textual readers say so. Delitzsch counts twelve lay houses here and in the Greek book of Esdras, ten of the names identical in both, and then lists what is odd: the first entry carries two family formulas where every other carries one, and at two later points a formula is followed not by a man's name but only by son of so-and-so. His conclusion is that the personal names have dropped out, and he takes the Greek evidence as corroboration. Ellicott reaches the same verdict independently at the first of those places, saying flatly that a name is omitted and that the Greek supplies it. Wesley, meanwhile, reads past the arithmetic to the households behind it: though only the males are expressed, doubtless they carried the women along with them, as they did the little ones.
10: The verse as it stands names a house and a leader, but one of the two names has fallen out of the Hebrew. Ellicott marks it in passing — here also a name is wanting — and the phrase here also points back to the same defect a few verses earlier, where a family formula was likewise followed by a patronymic with no personal name attached to it. The Greek translators had a fuller text, or supplied one, reading of the sons of Bani, Shelomith, the son of Josiphiah. On that reading Shelomith is not the clan but the man, Bani is the house he belonged to, and the hundred and sixty males counted with him are the men of that house who went up under him.
13:
Two words in the register carry more weight than their size. Ellicott explains the last sons of Adonikam as the younger branches of that house, the elder having been reported in the register of the first return. Wesley takes the same phrase as a closing of the account: it seems the rest came before, so that now all the sons of that family returned, and none stayed behind.

Delitzsch closes the list with arithmetic and a textual warning. Of the house of Bigvai two heads are named rather than one, and in the Greek book of Esdras those two names have been corrupted into a single unrecognisable form. He then totals the register both ways. The Hebrew yields fourteen hundred and ninety-six males and fifteen heads; the Greek yields sixteen hundred and ninety males and thirteen heads for the same twelve races. Neither figure includes the priests or the sons of David, whose numbers the chapter never states.

Where they assembled is disputed in a small way. Gill takes the river to have borne the name of the place it ran to, and links it with Adiabene, a district of Assyria named from the river Adiava. Clarke goes further and denies the distinction: Ahava was itself a river, probably the Diava or Adiava of that same province, and perhaps the home of the people of Ava whom the king of Assyria transplanted into Palestine. Ellicott holds both together — Ahava was river and town alike — and adds what neither of the others supplies, that nine days' journey brought the company there, and that a place now called Hit, some eighty miles from Babylon, has been identified with it. Delitzsch keeps to the grammar, noting that the phrase describes a river flowing toward or into Ahava, and that later in the chapter it is shortened simply to the river Ahava.

On what Ezra found missing the witnesses agree closely and press the point hard. Clarke reads none of the sons of Levi strictly: Ezra found priests, and priests are sons of Levi, but he found no Levites who were not priests. Wesley says the same and draws a consequence from it, that the Levites mentioned earlier in the book were named there by anticipation and had not yet joined him. Ellicott supplies the history that makes the absence intelligible: only seventy-four Levites had returned under Zerubbabel, so the disinclination was of long standing, and the importance of Levitical service in the temple accounts for Ezra's anxiety. Delitzsch simply reports the sequence — the company assembled, was ready to start, and Ezra perceived there were no Levites among them, whereupon he sent for the chief men and worked through Iddo's influence at Casiphia.

The deputation itself is described twice over, and the two accounts of its composition do not quite match. Gill counts eleven men sent for, three of them bearing the same name, and divides them: the first nine were men of chief note, rank and dignity in their families, while the last two were known for good sense and for being able to state a case well, which is why they were fit for this errand. Ellicott makes the same division but gives the last two an office rather than a temperament, calling them teachers and perhaps priests, joined to the nine as a deputation to Iddo.
17:
Where Casiphia lay is the sharpest disagreement in the chapter, and the distance at stake is enormous. Clarke reports that the most judicious commentators agree it means the Caspian mountains between Media and Hyrcania, and offers a reason the Nethinim would be settled there: the name comes from the word for silver, so they were probably employed working silver mines. Gill names that reading and rejects it on a practical ground — the Caspian was far too distant for messengers to go and return in the days the narrative allows. Following Jarchi, he puts Casiphia inside Babylon itself, a village on its edge or a street or parish within it, where Ezra knew many Levites and Nethinim lived and where Iddo was chief over both orders. Ellicott takes the same short view without the rabbinic authority: the place was evidently near Ahava, a Jewish colony presided over by Iddo, a man of the humble Nethinim who had risen to be chief under the Persians. He notes that Ezra was aware of their existence in those parts, which is why the errand was worth attempting at all. On the word ministers Ellicott is brief and decisive: the term obviously takes in Levites and Nethinim together, not Levites only.

The errand succeeded, and both Gill and Wesley refuse to let the success look ordinary. Gill unfolds the good hand of our God into its parts — the design favoured, the messengers protected, those they were sent to inclined to use their interest and authority with the men under them, and those men in turn made willing. Wesley turns it forward into a general rule: where ministers have been wanting and the vacancies are well supplied, ascribe it to the good hand of God, who qualifies men for the service, inclines them to it, and opens a door for them.

One phrase in the list of arrivals is probably not a phrase at all. Ellicott argues that a man of understanding is a proper name, Ishsekel, and grounds the claim on the grammar: the and standing before Sherebiah requires a name to precede it, and Sherebiah was a Levite known from the later history. Delitzsch reaches the same conclusion from the same joining word.

The Nethinim raise two further questions. On their origin Gill lays out the alternatives without deciding: some take them for the Gibeonites whom Joshua assigned to the service of the sanctuary and David afterwards confirmed, while others hold them a different body altogether, added to those. Delitzsch describes their office rather than their descent — given by David and the princes to the Levites, made servants of the house for its lowest work. Ellicott points out something the others pass over, that this verse is the only place in scripture recording that David appointed them to aid the Levites at all.

Then the two close readers divide over the last clause. Delitzsch takes all of them were expressed by name to mean that they were men of note, distinguished by name. Ellicott flatly denies it: not, as some think, that they were all famous, but that Iddo sent their names in a list which the narrative does not reproduce. What the relief of their coming was owed to, Ellicott adds, the text itself says — the good hand of our God upon us.
21:
Henry puts the fast where the narrative puts it, immediately after the recruiting succeeded, and draws the connection out: Ezra has procured Levites to go along with him, but what will that avail unless he have God with him? That is therefore his chief care.

Why Ezra would not ask for a military escort is explained the same way by three of the witnesses, Henry at greatest length. Ezra had told the king the principles he went on, that those who seek God are safe under the shadow of his wings even in their greatest dangers, while those who forsake him are exposed even when they feel most secure; having said that, he was ashamed to ask for a convoy, lest he give the king and the court occasion to suspect either God's power or his own confidence in it. Henry then guards the point against misuse. Those who depend on God must still use proper means for their preservation, and need not be ashamed to do so; the case is different only where the honour of God is directly concerned, and there a man should rather expose himself. Clarke reads it as a matter of consistency: having represented his God as supremely powerful and strongly affectionate toward his true followers, Ezra could not turn round and ask for soldiers, since failure afterwards would let the heathen conclude that the religion he professed was false and vain. Gill supplies the detail that makes the refusal cost something: Ezra could have had the band of soldiers and horsemen merely by asking, so great was his standing with the king.

On what the fast was for, Wesley and Henry agree almost word for word. Public mercies require public prayers, so that all who are to share the comfort may share in the asking; and the afflicting of themselves was for their sins, that they might be qualified for pardon. The rule both draw from it is the same — entering a new condition of life, take care to carry none of the guilt of the old one into it.

The right way they sought is read at two levels. Delitzsch keeps to the Hebrew: a straight way is a road made level by the clearing away of obstructions, which is to say a prosperous journey. Henry takes it as an act of self-commitment to the guidance of providence, and notes what made it necessary — they were strangers on the road, marching through their enemies' countries, and had no pillar of cloud and fire to lead them as their fathers had; they believed instead that the favour of God and the ministration of his angels would serve in its place. Ellicott names the danger they were guarding against, the wilderness ahead and an enemy the text leaves indefinite, most likely desert tribes lying in wait for unprotected caravans.

Two words in the petition get their own notes. Delitzsch takes the little ones as a collective term, properly the small children but more often the whole household, a man's wives and children together, and the substance as possessions in cattle and goods. Ellicott hears in the first an intimation that whole households went up, and takes the second to mean chiefly the temple treasure, though the word covers cattle and other property with an undertone of abundance. Delitzsch also refuses a common rendering in the sentence Ezra had quoted to the king: his power and his wrath is not a single phrase meaning powerful wrath, but names two things, the might that conquers every enemy and the anger in which it falls on the wicked. Wesley closes where the narrative does, with the plain report that God gave them an assurance of his gracious answer.
24:
Henry sees the sequence as the point. Having committed the keeping of the treasure to God, Ezra committed it to proper men whose business it was to watch it — though without God they would have waked in vain. Our prayers, Henry says, must always be seconded with our endeavours. He notices too which part of the baggage got the special guard: Ezra had prayed for all their substance, but it is the portion belonging to the house of God that he secures by name. The lesson Henry draws from that is a trade: if we expect God to keep by his providence what belongs to us, let us by his grace keep what belongs to him.

Who the guardians were raises a grammatical dispute the English hides. Ellicott renders the clause to Sherebiah, making the two named Levites, with ten others, partners with an equal number of priests in the charge. Delitzsch refuses that reading and gives his reasons: Sherebiah and Hashabiah were not priests nor chiefs of priests but Levites of the race of Merari, and so cannot be counted among the twelve chiefs of priests at all; and to take the particle as a dative would place the priests in a servile relation to the Levites, contrary to their standing. Gill, working from the number rather than the grammar, concludes that more priests had come up than the two the register names, and supposes their families or some of their brethren were with them.

Why the treasure was weighed rather than counted draws two different answers, and they fit together. Gill makes it a matter of Ezra's own exposure: he weighed it as proof of his integrity, as security against any later charge of embezzlement, as an example to the men receiving it, so that they should be under no temptation, and so that they could be vindicated if ever accused. Henry makes it a matter of accounting: Ezra weighed it because he expected to have it back by weight, and he notes the change from the first return, when the vessels were delivered by number and here by weight, so that anything missing would be apparent at once. Henry also records the reason Ezra himself gave for choosing these men — you are holy unto the Lord, and the vessels are holy also — and asks who could be fitter to take care of holy things than holy persons.

What the treasure was worth is where the witnesses diverge most widely. Ellicott says the gold and silver were carried in bars, and puts the silver at about a quarter of a million of our money and the gold at about three quarters of a million. Clarke reckons by talent and arrives close to the same place, six hundred and fifty talents of silver at four hundred and fifty pounds the talent making two hundred and ninety-two thousand five hundred, and the whole consignment something over a million pounds sterling, while noting that these weights and coins are variously computed and that other scales would halve his silver figure. Gill, following Scheuchzer, gives a figure more than twice as large, over two million two hundred thousand pounds sterling for the silver alone.

On one item Gill and Clarke contradict each other outright. Gill reports from Jarchi and Aben Ezra that there were a hundred silver vessels, each weighing a talent. Clarke denies precisely this: the weight of all the silver vessels together amounted to a hundred talents, not a hundred vessels of a talent apiece. Delitzsch stays with the text rather than the totals, noting that the offering is set in apposition to the metals, and that all Israel there present means those Israelites found in Babylon who were not themselves going up.
27:
The golden basons are valued by the same coin from two directions. Gill identifies the drams as Persian darics and reaches upwards of a thousand pounds of our money, citing Cumberland for the weight of the coin and Bernard for the comparison that it exceeded an English guinea by two grains. Ellicott names the coin the same way and states the total as rather more than a thousand guineas, which is the same sum arrived at from the other end.

The two vessels of fine copper, precious as gold, are a harder matter, and here the witnesses genuinely do not know. Ellicott ventures the Roman orichalcum, a metal very highly valued in antiquity. Clarke admits at the outset that what these were we cannot tell, and reports the Syriac, which renders them vessels of the best Corinthian brass — so called from the metal said to have been found after the burning of Corinth, where brass, copper, gold and silver were supposed to have run together in the fire. Clarke does not believe the legend. He thinks it was more likely a manufactured alloy made in that place, which took a polish and assumed the brightness of gold and was harder and so more durable; and he says such a metal is still made among the Asiatics, that he has watched it made, and that he kept a specimen exposed to every variation of the weather, even among old iron, for twenty years together with hardly any tarnish. The art of it is difficult, he adds, though the materials are of small value, and the result is widely different from the ormolu of France and England, less expensive and much more valuable.

On the charge Ezra gave with the treasure, Gill and Ellicott make the same connection between the men and the metal. Gill takes the holiness of the vessels to mean they were dedicated and set apart to sacred service, and therefore not to be converted to any other use. Ellicott calls the verse unique in every respect and states the principle it turns on: the treasures were consecrated, and they were committed to consecrated hands, with a good account to be rendered of them to the treasurers of the house.

The instruction itself is practical. Gill reads watch ye and keep them as a charge that the vessels, the gold and the silver be neither damaged nor diminished on the road. Delitzsch fills in the terms of the handover: they were to keep them until they should weigh them at Jerusalem before the chiefs of the priests, the Levites and the fathers of Israel, in the chambers of the house. And when the priests and Levites are said to have taken the weight of the silver and gold, Delitzsch explains that the phrase means they received it by weight, so that the same measure would settle the account at both ends of the journey. Gill adds only the count of the men who took it, the twelve priests and twelve Levites already named.
31:
The date of departure creates a small problem, and Delitzsch is the one who states it. The company left the river on the twelfth day of the first month, yet the journey from Babylon had been appointed for the first day of that month, and the encampment at the river lasted three days. His reconciliation runs like this: the travellers began assembling on the first day, and it was during the three days' encampment that Ezra discovered no Levites were among them, whereupon he sent the deputation to Casiphia; only when those men returned with their recruits did he proclaim the fast, and only then could the march begin. The nine missing days are the recruiting. Gill supplies a different bearing on the same date, that the twelfth of Nisan, answering to part of March and part of April, fell two days before the passover began.

How long the road took is given three ways. Delitzsch computes three months and a half, from the twelfth day of the first month to arrival on the first day of the fifth, and then admits what cannot be computed: the particulars of the journey are not recorded, and since the site of the river Ahava is unknown, the distance travelled cannot be determined at all. Henry reckons about four months and explains the slowness by the size of the party, whose numbers made the marches slow and the stages short.

On the preservation of the company the commentators agree and differ only in temperature. Ellicott is briefest: the hand of our God was upon us sums up the history of the whole journey. Henry unfolds what they were preserved from — enemies who lay in wait along the road to do them a mischief, or at least, like Amalek, to smite the hindmost of them — and turns it into a standing obligation, that even the common perils of ordinary journeys oblige us to sanctify our going out with prayer and our coming home with thanksgiving, and how much more an expedition as exposed as this one. On their safe arrival Henry adds an encouragement for those who have set their faces toward the new Jerusalem, that he who began the good work will perform it.

The three days of rest at the end are read slightly differently. Gill and Delitzsch both make them recovery: before going about any business the travellers took the rest that so fatiguing a journey made proper, remaining, as Delitzsch puts it, quiet and inactive, exactly as Nehemiah would afterwards do on his own arrival. Ellicott keeps the parallel with Nehemiah but will not leave the days empty, assigning them to rest and to more private devotion together.

The handover on the fourth day is described with the same exactness that governed the loading. Delitzsch names the four men who received the treasure, two priests and two Levites, with the chiefs of the priests and Levites present as the earlier charge required, and observes that one of them, Meremoth the son of Uriah, turns up again in the later history. Ellicott makes the same observation of the whole group of names. What was written down at the time, Delitzsch insists, was an authentic list: everything was delivered by number and by weight, and the whole weight was recorded then and there. Henry reads the scene from the carriers' side. They were impatient to be discharged of their trust, applied to the great men of the temple, and received an acquittance in full — for it is a great ease to a man's mind to be discharged from a trust, and a great honour to his name to be able to show that he discharged it faithfully.
35:
Delitzsch places the sacrifice in its sequence: the dedicated gifts having been delivered, the sons of the captivity offered burnt offerings and sin offerings out of gratitude for the gracious restoration of the people. He reads the numbers as deliberate. Twelve bullocks stand for all Israel, that is for the twelve tribes, and twelve he goats are the sin offering; the ninety-six rams he counts as eight times twelve, and the seventy-seven lambs as seven intensified. He also notes the order of the rites, the sin offering preceding the burnt offering as the necessary basis of an acceptable burnt offering, the one availing as atonement for the sins of all Israel and the other signifying the surrender of the whole. And he presses the last clause of the verse, that all this was a burnt offering, meaning that nothing of it could be eaten by those who brought it.

What the twelve bullocks meant when ten of the tribes were gone is answered two ways. Clarke faces the arithmetic directly: of tribes there were only Judah and Benjamin, yet a bullock was offered for every tribe as if present. He will not go so far as to say the others were unrepresented — there can be little doubt that individuals from all twelve were there, possibly some families of each — but no complete tribe beyond the two. Wesley takes the same numbers as evidence of something recovered rather than something absent. The twelve bullocks, the twelve goats and the ninety-six rams signify the union of the two kingdoms: they no longer went two tribes one way and ten another, but all twelve met by their representatives at the same altar. On the sin offering itself Wesley repeats the rule he applies throughout, that it is the atonement which secures every mercy to us, and that no mercy is truly comfortable until iniquity is taken away and our peace made with God.

Ellicott sees an order of precedence in the closing verses and says so plainly. The burnt offerings came first; then, having rendered to God the things that were God's, they rendered to Caesar the things that were Caesar's, and delivered the royal commission to the officers who had to act on it.

Who those officers were is set out with some care. Ellicott distinguishes the two ranks, the lieutenants or satraps holding military authority and the governors, the pechahs or pashas, holding civil authority under them, and observes that the commission was of course accepted and acted upon, since the text says they furthered the people. Delitzsch draws the same line between military chiefs and heads of the civil government, and glosses the verb rendered furthered as to lift up, to support. Gill identifies the territory rather than the ranks: these were the governors of the provinces of Syria, Palestine and Judea, which lay on that side of the great river.

Clarke, characteristically, goes at the word for lieutenants and then admits defeat. It is generally understood to mean a deputy, is probably Persian in origin, and is here greatly corrupted; the Latin renders it satraps. He canvasses Persian candidates — the term for a viceroy, a word meaning a person in whom one has confidence, an epithet belonging to a vizir — and then withdraws them all, saying he gives none of these etymologies with confidence, and that where there is so little certainty conjecture is useless. He adds, drily, that a dissertation might be written on the Persian words and forms of speech in these books, but that probably few of his readers would thank him for the toil.
